title: Friday: the hour of answer
hook: an hour on Friday when du'a is answered (Bukhari)
tomorrow: what does a Friday sound like, counted on ten fingers?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the friday light: al-Kahf, read weekly, resetting how you count the days. Today the count gets small. One hour, maybe less.

A sale drops at a random minute, and people refresh all day so they don't miss it. Friday has an older version. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ speaks of an hour on Friday: if a Muslim standing in prayer asks God for something good in it, God gives it. Then he gestures with his hand, showing how short it is. And the report never says when.
screen: `REFRESH ALL DAY.` → `AN HOUR ON FRIDAY.` → `SHORT, AND UNNAMED.`

segments.voice: Two answers, each with a report behind it. The first comes from Abu Musa, in Sahih Muslim: the hour falls between the moment the imam sits on the pulpit and the end of the prayer. Its case is simple and strong. That's when the community is gathered, listening, already in worship. If any stretch of Friday is open, why not the one where everyone stands together? The second comes from Jabir, in Sunan Abi Dawud: seek it in the last hour of Friday, after 'Asr, before sunset. There's an objection. The report says standing in prayer, and after 'Asr is a time when voluntary prayer isn't made. A companion, Abdullah ibn Salam, gave the reply people still quote: whoever sits waiting for the prayer is counted as in prayer. So someone sitting with their du'a in the late afternoon, waiting for Maghrib, is inside the promise. Scholars gathered these two views, and others besides. Some concluded the hour is hidden on purpose, the way someone who doesn't know which minute matters stays awake for all of them. And some people simply keep both windows: quiet attention during the sermon, and du'a in the last light before sunset. That's the hidden hour: not a code to crack, but a reason to keep asking.
screen: `ABU MUSA: PULPIT TO PRAYER'S END.` · `JABIR: THE LAST HOUR, AFTER 'ASR.` · `WAITING FOR PRAYER IS PRAYER.` · `HIDDEN, SO YOU KEEP ASKING.` · then, large: `THE HIDDEN HOUR.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write, by hand, one good thing you'd ask for if you knew the hour had come. Keep it short and honest. If you pray, keep the paper for Friday's last light; if not, keep it where you'll see it, as a note of what you're hoping for.
screen: `ONE GOOD THING, BY HAND.` · `SHORT AND HONEST.` · `KEEP IT FOR FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: Friday's hidden hour: a short time, unnamed in the main report, when a sincere du'a is answered; the reports point to two windows.
One to keep: the hidden hour isn't a code to crack, it's a reason to keep asking. Day three of the week, done.

screen: `DAY 1683 COUNTS.` → `THE WEEKLY RHYTHM · 3 OF 7.` → `TOMORROW: A FRIDAY, COUNTED ON TEN FINGERS.`

howItsDone: Muslims who seek the Friday hour make du'a during the sermon and prayer, and again in the late afternoon after 'Asr, some sitting quietly in the mosque or at home until Maghrib.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 935 (an hour on Friday; a Muslim standing in prayer asking for good is given it; he pointed with his hand to show how short it is)
Sahih Muslim 853 (Abu Musa: between the imam sitting and the end of the prayer)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1048 (Jabir: seek it in the last hour after 'Asr)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1046; Muwatta Malik, Book of Friday (Abdullah ibn Salam: whoever sits waiting for the prayer is in prayer)
Sahih al-Bukhari 586 (no voluntary prayer after 'Asr until sunset)

notes: Debate day: the two views are given their best case each; neither is ranked. Confirm the numbering of Muslim 853, Abu Dawud 1048 and 1046 (Abdullah ibn Salam's exchange with Abu Hurayra; also in the Muwatta and Tirmidhi).
'Scholars gathered these two views, and others besides' stays general on purpose (Ibn Hajar lists many more in Fath al-Bari; no count given).
'After 'Asr is a time when voluntary prayer isn't made': general statement of the prohibited times; confirm phrasing.
